dissented.against: Claim 4, second half: agent names resolve to a fixpoint rather than matching a pattern.
dissented.finding: Six reachable constructions dispatch to sov-witness with the builder's account named as the oracle, and sovprompts.audit.violations returns [] for every one. Each was placed as live code above sov-loop.js's final top-level return, and each was first executed in node with a recording stub to confirm it really calls agent with agentType 'sov-witness' and the oracle prompt. The six: hG1['spawn'] = agent then hG1.spawn(...); const hG2 = { send: agent } then hG2['send'](...); await (0, agent)(...); const arrG = [agent] then arrG[0](...); const bG = agent.bind(null) then bG(...); const tG = true ? agent : null then tG(...).
dissented.cause: calls._agent_names resolves by comparing a written expression, or its dotted tail, for equality with a name already in the set. Any expression that merely contains the token agent - a ternary, a .bind() call, an array literal, a comma expression - is not equal to it and is not resolved. A computed member write or read never enters _writes_by_name at all, because masked() blanks the string subscript and no identifier then abuts the '='.
dissented.consequence: The docstring on _agent_names states: 'Four alias shapes were closed case by case and the class came back one hop further... which is why this has to be resolution to a fixpoint rather than a pattern.' Graded as a claim, that is false. The fixpoint is over exact-string and dotted-tail equality, which is pattern matching one level up, and the class is still open one hop further - for the ninth time. Two of the six (the computed-member pair) are named in bindings.py's stated ceiling; the other four fall only under that ceiling's closing clause, 'any construction a JavaScript engine would evaluate but this does not', which covers everything and cannot be defeated. A ceiling that cannot be defeated is not a ceiling.
dissented.severity: material, not blocking. The 23 shipped workflows contain none of these six shapes; agent_calls enumerates every real dispatch correctly today. This is a guard that does not hold, not a live breach of the rule.

dissented.against: Claim 3, scan.py is the single mask for the package and no reader keeps a private scanner that disagrees with it.
dissented.finding: At least eight private character scanners remain across four modules: dispatch.prompt_of, dispatch.interpolated, bindings._statement, bindings._balanced, bindings._split_arguments, calls._object_member, render._literals, and lexer.py, which is a second tokenizer in full. bindings._balanced and calls._object_member do not skip string literals at all; dispatch.interpolated understands ' and " but not backticks or regex literals.
dissented.demonstrated_disagreement: render._body('function f(x) { const b = \'}\' ; return \'ORACLE\' + x.summary }', 'f') returns " const b = '" - it truncates at a close brace inside a string literal, which masked() would have blanked. And lexer.VALUE_ENDERS treats '}' as a value-ender, so a '/' after it divides, while scan.BEFORE_REGEX contains '}', so the same '/' opens a regex. Given a function whose body holds `if (x) { }` on one line and `/'/.test(x)` on the next - JavaScript node parses without complaint - lexer.unreadable returns "line 4: a ' string is not closed before the line ends". The check falsely convicts legal JavaScript.
dissented.consequence: lexer.py's docstring says 'The word list that says a regex may follow now comes from scan.py, so this reader and the mask cannot drift apart again - their disagreeing is what produced the defect.' Only the word list is shared. The character rules still disagree, on '}', and the disagreement still produces the exact failure the docstring says was repaired. Nothing in the 23 shipped workflows triggers it, so this is a latent build-stopper rather than a current one. I could not turn any of these disagreements into a missed refusal - every path I tried failed closed into a different refusal - so the package is currently safe for a reason it does not state.

is_this_a_coherent_design: The centre is coherent and the perimeter is an accumulation, and this candidate moves the boundary between them in the right direction without reaching it. Three things here are genuine structure and they hold under attack: one predicate read in both directions, a corpus that puts refusals in the tree rather than in docstrings, and a frame that grades position inside the block that owns each instruction. The position rule in particular survived every attack I could construct - template literal, array join, helper call, const-held tail, const-held whole prompt - and that is not what an accumulation looks like. What remains an accumulation is everything lexical. Four readers of JavaScript still coexist: one mask, one tokenizer, and half a dozen ad-hoc character scans inside the resolvers. They already disagree, demonstrably, on the '}' character and on a brace inside a string literal. The enumerator is where that accumulation shows: six one-hop constructions still escape it, and each new hop has been closed by name for nine readings running. The disputed structural work - making the frame the only way to build a witness prompt - would remove the presence rule that twenty workflows currently rely on, and it is the only repair that addresses the class rather than the instance. On the question readings six, seven and eight split over: I side with seven and eight that it is owed, but I record as fact that no workflow file in this tree imports anything, so the refactor would introduce cross-file imports into a format that has none, and neither the builder nor I can verify from here that the host supports them. That is a real dependency seam, not an excuse. It should be asked as a capability question before the refactor is planned, not discovered during it.

grant:standing-landing-loop admits diagrams/ and docs/ but excludes STATUS.yaml, decisions/ and .clarity/coverage.json - the sources those derived artifacts are pinned against. This candidate is a worked instance: a change entirely inside the grant's scope cannot be landed under the grant without a companion change the grant forbids. decisions/0104 names the class; does the owner want the grant widened, the derived artifacts excluded from it, or candidates of this shape routed to acceptance by rule?

No contract in contracts/ admits the six top-level keys scripts/sovkernel/authority.py and scripts/sovland/candidates.py read out of an observation, and nothing grades reports/observations/ against a schema. Which side is wrong, the gate or the schemas? Unrouted after nine records.

Is MEASURED the right token for sovkernel.authority.independence_basis to write into the landing ledger, when what it establishes is that an observation was supplied from a path the caller resolved and not that its observer stayed outside the build? The docstring is honest; the enum value is the thing a later reader will quote.

Nine independent readings have now each defeated this guard one layer further out, and three observers have retired themselves for lost independence. Is iterating this check to a fixpoint the right expenditure, or is the frame-as-sole-constructor refactor the point at which the class stops recurring? That is a resource-commitment question, not an engineering one, and the dependency seam named in is_this_a_coherent_design has to be answered first.
